title: Observer pattern
idea: The Observer pattern lets a subject keep a list of observers and notify each one when something happens, without knowing their concrete classes.

analogy.text: You subscribe to a newsletter. The publisher mails each issue to its whole list and never learns what each reader does with it.
analogy.breaks: Here delivery is a direct call: a slow reader stalls the publisher.

points: Observers implement one interface; the subject loops over its list and calls each.
New reactions subscribe at runtime, so the subject stays closed for modification.
The JDK has `PropertyChangeListener`; `java.util.Observer` is deprecated since Java 9.
Skip it when one fixed collaborator always reacts; a direct call is clearer.

steps.caption: Four observers subscribe. The subject stores them only as `BuildListener` references.
Build 41 passes. The subject calls every observer in order; pager and alert ignore it.
Build 42 fails. Chat posts first, then the loop reaches the pager.
The pager throws. The subject catches it around that one call and keeps going.
The alert fires, then unsubscribes itself mid-loop. `CopyOnWriteArrayList` makes that safe.
The dashboard still updates. One broken observer did not stop the others.
Build 43 fails. The alert is gone from the list, so only three observers are called.

code.title: The problem: hard-wired calls
code.caption: The build server calls each interested class by name, in one fixed method.

walk.text: The subject holds three concrete classes and cannot be reused without them.
Every reaction is a hard-coded call. Adding audit or metrics means editing this method.
The pager throws, so the dashboard update on the next line never runs.
The failure escapes to the caller: one broken dependency crashes the whole build step.

code.title: The fix: subscribed observers
code.caption: Observers subscribe through one interface; the subject isolates failures and allows removal.

walk.text: The event is an immutable record, so no observer can change what the others see.
Observers share one small interface. Lambdas fit because it has a single method.
`CopyOnWriteArrayList` iterates a snapshot, so removing during a notify is safe.
Subscribe and unsubscribe at runtime; `requireNonNull` rejects a null listener at the door.
Each call has its own try/catch, so one failing observer cannot starve the rest.
A one-shot observer removes itself mid-loop. With a plain `ArrayList` that is a bug.
`main` wires four observers; the subject never learns their classes.

pitfalls: Never unsubscribing keeps dead observers reachable: a lapsed-listener memory leak that grows over time.
Removing an observer from an `ArrayList` mid-loop can skip the next one or throw.
A slow observer blocks the subject; hand slow work to an executor or a queue.

quiz.why: Removing `once` shrinks the list to two while the iterator's cursor sits at 2. `hasNext` returns false, so `log` is silently skipped.

takeaway: The subject announces; observers decide. Neither knows the other's class.

starters: Why was java.util.Observer deprecated, and what should I use instead?
How do I make observers asynchronous without losing events?
How is the Observer pattern different from a message queue or pub/sub?
